prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms brought optical atomic clocks to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B029, Katori and Ye. After the first round I regard the case as stronger than I argued it, because the main objection (overlap with 2005 and 2012) has been put to it by every supporter and I think it can be answered on physics. Hall and Haensch were honoured for the frequency comb, the tool that counts optical cycles; Wineland and Haroche for control of single quantum systems, including single-ion clocks. A single ion gives an excellent standard but a statistical limit set by one particle. Katori's idea is that at the magic wavelength the light shift of the clock transition cancels, so thousands of neutral atoms can be held Lamb-Dicke confined, free of Doppler and recoil shifts, without the trap perturbing the transition. That moves the trade-off between stability and systematic uncertainty and is what lets averaging times fall by orders of magnitude. Ye's group then took the strontium lattice to the 10^-18 level, with the blackbody radiation shift controlled at the corresponding level, and into spin-resolved and many-body clock operation. This is a distinct experimental architecture that I can judge from my own field, not a refinement of the comb or of ion control. Maturity rests on the demonstrated performance: several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST) have reproduced and intercompared lattice clocks at the 10^-17 to 10^-18 level, and the clocks already work as instruments, for example in height measurements through the gravitational redshift. I do not rest the case on the redefinition of the second or on a future violation of a constant.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is a real reservation and the committee is entitled to weigh it; my answer is that the lattice scheme is a separate achievement, but a member who reads the clock as the continuation of one lineage is not being unreasonable. Second, a two-name credit simplifies a crowded field: Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, Hinkley, Bloom, Schiller and the Yb lattice and Al+ ion-clock groups reached comparable accuracy, and the 10^-18 milestone is not Ye's alone. I therefore want the citation to credit the concept and its realisation and not a record number that several groups hold. Third, Pearce is right that the tests of fundamental physics are still mostly prospective, and the first-round wording I used, 'opening new tests of fundamental physics and a path to redefining the second', leaned on that. I have removed it. Fourth, Danielsson is right that a tidy credit assignment is not a substitute for the importance of the finding, and the Higgs is a discovery about nature where the clock is a measurement advance. I judge that the Higgs case is stronger in significance but weaker as a prize configuration, because I still cannot see a principle that selects three people from two collaborations.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B012 (Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee) as his first choice, calls the Higgs an actual discovery about nature, and treats B029 as a strong alternative that he would not contest vigorously, while saying that a tidy credit should not outrank the importance of the finding.
responses.response: I accept that the importance of the Higgs is not in doubt and I do not weigh it below the clocks as physics. Where we differ is on what a prize citation has to do. A citation must name who did the work that is being honoured. Your own text concedes that spokespersons at the time of the announcement, detector pioneers and accelerator leaders have comparable claims, and I have not heard a stated rule that makes Jenni, Della Negra and Virdee the three. Conception and construction leadership is real, but the citation you propose honours that, not the analysis that found the boson. If you can state the decisive individual contribution, or reformulate so that the citation does not need three founders from several thousand people, I would reconsider. As it stands I would place B012 behind B029 on attribution alone. I also disagree that the clock is only a precision refinement: the claim that it is a separate and demonstrated capability does not depend on the future, and I have dropped the redefinition and the fundamental-physics language so the comparison is fair.

responses.point: Pearce supports B029 but says that new physics from the clock is still mostly prospective, since nobody has yet used it to find a violation of a fundamental constant, and wants the citation built on demonstrated precision and the new capability.
responses.response: I accept this and it changes my wording. My round-1 citation included new tests of fundamental physics and a path to redefining the second, and both are consequences that have not been delivered. The revised citation rests on the invention, the magic-wavelength mechanism and the demonstrated 10^-18 uncertainty with independent intercomparison. I would keep one factual point in the argument but not in the citation: clocks at this level are already used for relativistic geodesy through the redshift between laboratories, which is a use that exists and not an expectation. On your chair question about Katori and Ye against other groups, my answer is that Katori proposed and first demonstrated the magic-wavelength lattice and Ye's group made the strontium clock the reference at 10^-18, and these two roles are separable from the later Yb, Al+ and European results. If the committee preferred to add a third name I would want a specific contribution identified, and I do not think it changes anything for me if it does not.

responses.point: Lindroth supports the same two names and asks that the citation name the lattice clock concept and its realisation, not a record number that Sr, Yb and Al+ groups share, and she separates the Hall/JILA connection from the merit of the result.
responses.response: I agree with your wording point and have adopted it: the new citation names the concept (magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms) and its realisation, and mentions 10^-18 as the level reached, not as a priority claim. I also accept your reading that the Hall/JILA association bears on a career and not on the merit, since the result is reproduced by groups with no JILA link. Where I still differ from you slightly is on B018 as the fallback. I had it as my first alternative, but after reading Johansson and Eriksson on the 2012 overlap and the NIST and Monroe credit gap, I would put it as a weaker fallback than I did in round 1. If B029 does not hold, I would want the committee to say what the Cirac-Zoller proposal adds beyond Wineland's prize before voting for it.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B035 (DMFT) on originality, but now says he ranked B029 too low and would support it as a prize, while thinking that DMFT is the more fundamental new idea and that precision metrology partly follows from the comb and ion-control prizes.
responses.response: I appreciate that you say you would support B029 and I take your point that DMFT is conceptually deeper. I do not think depth of concept and ability to credit are the same test, and you yourself call the Metzner gap real; a prize that omits the originator of the infinite-dimension limit would not be sound. On kind versus quality: I would resist the idea that clocks are only a consequence of the comb. The comb makes an optical clock countable, but whether the atoms are many, trapped and shift-free is a separate experimental result, and the 2005 citation did not cover it. I do not see this as a ranking of fundamental over applied, since the clock was one of the cleanest cases in which a measurement advance came from a new physical idea.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; my judgement rests on the architecture (many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength) and I cannot prove it to a member who reads the clocks as one lineage.

Whether Katori and Ye are the right two names given comparable work by Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, Hinkley, Bloom, Schiller and the Yb and Al+ groups; I cannot resolve the priority question from the supplied record beyond Katori's proposal and Ye's strontium results.
Whether to wait for the redefinition of the second: I do not treat it as a scientific criterion, but I recognise that others weigh it differently.

If B029 fails, I am unsure which fallback is better. B018 has the Wineland overlap and the NIST and Monroe credit gap; B004 has an unresolved choice of triple from Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff and the 2025 circuits prize.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. My profile records a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my doctoral period, and Jun Ye's career is tied to the Hall and JILA environment. It documents no collaboration, supervision or shared funding with Ye or Katori, and I know of no other tie. In round 1 I asked the committee to judge this and several members have since answered. My own view is that it is a disclosure and does not require recusal: the link is to a laboratory and a period, not to a credited person, Hall's own recognition in 2005 concerns the comb, not the lattice clock, and the result is reproduced by groups with no JILA tie. I would accept the committee's decision if it asked me to stand aside, and note that Johansson, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson and Pearce reached B029 independently, so the outcome does not depend on my vote. I have field-level proximity to the AMO candidates B018, B004 and B044 as an atomic physicist and member of the Lund quantum-information community, and for that reason I would not use my own weight to promote any of them. I note I am also a member of the rare-earth-ion quantum-memory community and have WACQT and Deep Light Vision involvement; none concerns a shortlisted name.
